definition: Disaffected means rebellious, discontented, and disloyal toward those in authority.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disaffected. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disaffected should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After management broke its promise of safer equipment for the third time, the once loyal assembly crew grew openly disaffected, ignoring directives and talking of walking out.
A dissatisfied employee grumbles about conditions, but a disaffected one has stopped feeling any loyalty to the employer at all.
Disaffected groups withhold loyalty and trust, while a mutinous group has moved beyond that into open revolt against its leaders.

Rebellious describes active resistance to authority - breaking rules, defying orders, pushing back. Disaffected describes the state that usually comes first: loyalty and trust in the authority have drained away. A rebellious crew is already fighting back; a disaffected crew has stopped feeling loyal and may or may not ever act on it.

Alienated means feeling cut off and estranged, an outsider with no real bond left - to a family, a culture, a workplace, anything. Disaffected is narrower and points at an authority or institution: the loyalty once given to a government or employer has turned to resentment. You can feel alienated from everything; you become disaffected with something you once followed.

Discontented means unhappy with your circumstances - the pay, the conditions, the way things are going. Disaffected goes further than mood: it means loyalty itself has broken down. Workers can be discontented yet still loyal to the company; disaffected workers have withdrawn that loyalty and turned resentful toward it.

Disaffected is about lost loyalty, not just low spirits.
It describes people, often groups, who have turned resentful and rebellious toward an authority such as a government, employer, or school.
Unlike disheartened, which describes lost hope or morale after a setback, disaffected specifically implies that loyalty toward an institution has broken down.

For decades the mill town's football club could count on the north stand: three generations of families who sang through relegations and rain.
Then an investment group bought the club, doubled ticket prices, and moved kickoff times to suit television.
The supporters did not riot or even stop attending; most still came, out of habit as much as love.
But they had become disaffected.
The songs grew quieter, the club scarves stayed home, and when the chairman's name appeared on the screen, the stand answered with silence.
Loyalty, once given freely for generations, had been withdrawn, and everyone in the boardroom knew it.
